sections.html:
• Common name: Subwassertang
  • Other names: Süsswassertang, Süßwassertang, Loma fern, Round Pellia, False Round Pellia
  • Scientific name: none (genus Lomariopsis)
  • Minimum tank size: 10 litres
  • Difficulty: easy
  • Lighting: low to moderate
  • Substrate: any / floating
  • Growth rate: slow to moderate
  • Placement: foreground
  • Size: up to 20 cm or more
  • Fertilisers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: division
  • Colour: green

Subwassertang is a popular aquarium plant. It was long considered a liverwort because of its ribbon-like thallus, but it is not algae, moss or liverwort: it is the prothallium (gametophyte) of a fern. DNA analysis shows it is closely related to Lomariopsis lineata, but it has not been named as a distinct species and cannot be expressly regarded as Lomariopsis lineata, so it has no scientific name of its own.

It was introduced to the hobby by Christel Kasselman after its discovery in the early 2000s. She propagated it and gave some to other aquarists, and it spread among hobbyists worldwide. How the plant made its way into her aquarium is unknown.

Taxonomy: Kingdom Plantae, Class Polypodiopsida, Order Polypodiales, Family Lomariopsidaceae, Genus Lomariopsis, Species Lomariopsis sp. (the closest relative).

Biologists do not know much about this plant, and to date no record exists of the gametophytes of Lomariopsis lineata growing naturally in aquatic environments. Subwassertang and Lomariopsis lineata are presumed to be native to tropical Asia and Africa, where they grow on trees and hard surfaces, attaching firmly with numerous rhizoids. Subwassertang is epiphytic and also grows on rocks in periodically dry rivers.

Because there was only one known introduction into the aquatic trade, it can reasonably be assumed that all plants currently sold are exact clones of each other and have reproduced entirely by continuous meristematic growth.

The plant is a fern gametophyte that never develops further and keeps growing and replicating as a gametophyte. It strongly resembles the liverwort Monosolenium tenerum, wrongly called Pellia. It consists of branching ribbon-shaped thallus, thin like a membrane (one cell layer thick) with no midrib, with broad round lobes whose tips are never truncate. Beneath the thallus are rhizoids (hair-like organs that anchor the plant to hardscape or decorations), often grouped and located at irregular distances on the underside and near the margin. Compared with Monosolenium tenerum, the thallus of Subwassertang is more transparent, darker green, more flexible and less fragile.

Unlike most aquarium plants, Subwassertang needs little attention. Some aquarists do not even plant or attach it and simply throw it into the tank; it finds a spot it likes and grows. Because it grows without CO2 and fertiliser, it is a perfect choice for shrimp tanks and low-tech planted tanks.

Most care consists of routine partial water changes to balance water parameters and keep water quality good. Pruning is only needed after a long while. The plant grows slowly, but once established it can grow explosively. When clumps become too dense or out of shape, prune them to keep them compact.

Planting is easy and the plant can be shaped in many ways. It can float freely until it settles on a spot, or be attached to driftwood, rocks and pipes. To attach it to a piece of wood, spread a little Subwassertang over it, tie the clumps around a couple of times with black thread or fishing line, pass the thread through the loops to cover the whole area, then knot it. Pieces attached to tree-shaped driftwood form a "Süßwasser tree". Small portions can be pushed into a crevice in wood or rock so that it looks naturally grown there. Some hobbyists tie it to a slate pad and place it on the substrate to form a carpet, which is easier than placing it directly on gravel. Clumps can also be attached to an acrylic ledge held on the glass by suction cups, giving the illusion of plants floating in the tank.

Propagation is by division: break off small portions, attach them to hardscape and they grow into a new plant.

Disinfect it in a bleach or salt dip before placing it in the tank to reduce the chance of introducing pests and snails. However, because of its thin structure, it does not react well to dips and often turns brown, so dilute the dip. A weaker dip may not kill snails and other pests; keeping it in a quarantine tank for a few weeks is the best way to treat it.

Tank size: Subwassertang suits both nano and large tanks. The minimum tank size is 10 litres.

Temperature: it grows best at 20–24 °C. In nature it can thrive in cold temperatures.

pH: 6.0–8.0.

Hardness: it tolerates a wide range of hardness but prefers soft water, 0–8 dGH.

Lighting: medium lighting is ideal and gives more yield and faster growth. It also grows well in low light, at the expense of slightly slower growth and a duller appearance, though the bottom leaves stay fine. There are reports that it dislikes high light and can melt away.

Flow: it prefers medium flow. Strong flow makes it float around the tank and can break off parts of the plant.

CO2 and fertilisation: CO2 injection is not necessary, although it can increase growth a little. The plant does fine without liquid carbon and fertilisers. A high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilisers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp, so take care when adding it to a shrimp tank or a high-tech planted tank.

Subwassertang is perfect for shrimp tanks. Dense clumps give shrimp and fry hiding places and keep them safe from predators, and serve as a spawning and breeding place for egg scatterers. They also provide a foraging ground for baby shrimp and snails: the structure acts as a buffet of biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.

Compatible tankmates: peaceful fish such as Otocinclus catfish, pygmy Corydoras, neon tetras, guppies, cherry barbs, green swordtails, rasboras and platies; all shrimp, including Neocaridina (Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Black Rose, Snowball, Orange Sakura, Green Jade, Rili) and Caridina (Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti, Blue Tiger), as well as Amano, ghost, bamboo and vampire shrimp; and snails such as ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor and mystery snails, though care is needed with snails that may eat the plant.

Avoid hostile, aggressive diggers and voracious plant-eaters that will tear up plants, such as silver dollars, Oscars and other cichlids. Do not keep it with crayfish or crabs, which eat and uproot everything; floating plants are the better choice for those tanks.

Benefits: it can be shaped into a tree, carpet, ball or wall, with flexibility similar to Java moss, and can be used in the foreground if trimmed down well. It helps oxygenation and can remove excess nutrients, toxins and heavy metals, although this is low at first because it grows slowly. It is also an alternative for people who cannot grow mosses.

Common problems:

  • Slow start: it can take weeks or even months to adapt to new parameters, but grows quickly once established in good conditions.
  • Melting: plants gradually melt or smother if water parameters are unstable. Avoid drastic changes, keep low to medium light and keep the water clean.
  • Hard to attach: it has no roots and anchors with small rhizoids. Tie it loosely; tying too tightly crushes the plant and it can die where you want it to attach.
  • Fragile: small pieces break off easily when handled and spread through the tank, so it may slowly take over new areas.
  • Algae: it is susceptible to algae, especially hair algae in hard water, and intense light or long photoperiods encourage this.
  • Seachem Excel: it does not kill the plant but can slow its growth.
  • Disinfection: it often turns brown after dips because of its thin structure.

Buying: it is fairly rare and may be hard to find in local shops, but is easy to find online. Choose healthy portions, and always disinfect or quarantine the plant to avoid introducing snails, parasites, pests or pesticide residues.

Subwassertang is a hardy plant and a close substitute for the renowned Java moss. Shrimp are often seen hiding and roaming on its dense green foliage, which gives a lot of surface area for grazing.
